Title: [Excerpt from] Life at the Top
Author: by Dan Risch
Content: Upon this high plateau slung between the world's tallest mountains thrive the nomads of Tibet. Isolated from conveniences such as indoor plumbing, sturdy warm housing, and electricity, they've adapted to living in one of `text(Earth's)` harshest environments. They live in step with the environment. Moreover, scientists are discovering that even Tibetans' bodies have adapted to living at the world's edge.

The land's extremes arise from the mountains surrounding the plateau. Tibetan nomads live where trees can't grow, rivers don't exist, and `text(each breath)` of air has much less oxygen than a breath taken at sea level.

Breathing less oxygen stresses people. Called high altitude hypoxia (hi-POX-ee-uh), it causes headaches, fatigue, nausea, and loss of appetite. Someone experiencing hypoxia has lost their balance, but not in the sense of tripping. Their body has lost homeostasis.

Homeostasis (rhymes with Romeo-stay-sis) means keeping fluids within the body in balance. The high elevation of Tibet disrupts a person's homeostasis. Yet, Tibetans live healthy lives. Unique among all the people of the world (except for people living on the Ethiopian Plateau or in the Andes Mountains), Tibetans have developed adaptations to maintain homeostasis. Scientists refer to adaptations as cultural or physiological¹. Tibetans use both.

Dr. Cynthia Beall studies Tibetans' high altitude adaptations. She has lived with Tibet's yak, goat, and sheep herding nomads. She admires what she believes is the key to their cultural adaptations: living in harmony with nature.

She says that cold is a constant on the plateau. Deep winter temperatures fall to `30°` below `text(zero F)`. Summer temperatures rise to the `text(70s)`, in direct sunlight. In response to the cold, Tibetans stay outside when the sun shines. Their clothing and tent homes borrow their sheep's and yaks' natural protections against cold. They wear bathrobe-like coats with leather outside to repel wind and hail with fleece inside for insulation.

Seasonal shifts guide Tibetan herd management and food use. They move their herds to allow ... animals to eat the richest grasses when producing milk for newborn kids and lambs. They collect milk for themselves, too. They make food to store for later use. Buttermilk is used `text(first)`, then yogurt, a favorite food, and then butter and hard cheese, which lasts until the next milk-producing season.

As efficient as these cultural adaptations are, they alone don't allow Tibetans to live healthy lives. Dr. Beall has discovered within the Tibetans' bodies physiological adaptations that promote homeostasis in their high-altitude world.

`text(First)`, she found that Tibetans take a lot of breaths to move more oxygen into their bodies. In fact, Tibetans take `text(75 percent)` more breaths `text(per minute)` than someone at sea level.

But this adaptation still isn't enough to maintain homeostasis while living on the plateau. Dr. Beall recently discovered another physiological adaptation. Tibetans' blood circulates fast. Their blood vessels open very wide. This means that more blood picks up new oxygen from the lungs more frequently...
Altogether, these cultural and physiological adaptations allow Tibetans to survive life at the top of the world.
